title: Dramatis Personae

teacherSummary.text: The cast list divides Verona into the Prince's family (Escalus, his kinsmen Paris and Mercutio), the house of Montague (Montague, Lady Montague, Romeo, Benvolio and servants) and the house of Capulet (Capulet, Lady Capulet, Juliet, Tybalt, the Nurse and servants), with two Franciscan friars and an apothecary outside both. The scenes are Verona and Mantua.

context.history: Verona and Mantua were real cities in northern Italy; Italy was, for English audiences of the 1590s, a place of passion, feuds and fashionable duelling. The story came to Shakespeare through Arthur Brooke's English poem of 1562.

significance: Reading the cast first lets students see the feud's structure: two houses 'at variance', each with servants who fight for them, and a few figures (the Prince's kin, the Friar) who might bridge or break the divide.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Dramatis Personae,” how does Shakespeare show the divided world of Verona? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Dramatis Personae, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the divided world of Verona? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Dramatis Personae develops the idea of the divided world of Verona. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Dramatis Personae (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of the divided world of Verona. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Dramatis Personae suggests about the divided world of Verona. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and setting), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Dramatis Personae to complicate the reader's understanding of the divided world of Verona. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Dramatis Personae within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the divided world of Verona responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Dramatis Personae alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the divided world of Verona follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Dramatis Personae and its treatment of the divided world of Verona. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and setting, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Dramatis Personae as evidence for a larger claim about the divided world of Verona in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Dramatis Personae as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the divided world of Verona. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The cast list shows a city divided into camps, with only the Prince's kin standing outside the feud. Useful evidence: “Mercutio, kinsman to the prince, and friend to Romeo” (Dramatis Personae, speech (speech 0)): Mercutio stands between the Prince's family and the Montagues. Theme link: servants are listed by house; the quarrel reaches down to every household member. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: A critic might argue: “Reading the cast first lets students see the feud's structure: two houses 'at variance', each with servants who fight for them, and a few figures (the Prince's kin, the Friar) who might bridge or break the divide.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The cast list shows a city divided into camps, with only the Prince's kin standing outside the feud. Useful evidence: “Tybalt, nephew to Lady Capulet” (Dramatis Personae, speech (speech 0)): Tybalt's tie to Lady Capulet explains her later grief and demand for revenge. Theme link: servants are listed by house; the quarrel reaches down to every household member. items.text: Which character in this scene acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The cast list shows a city divided into camps, with only the Prince's kin standing outside the feud. Useful evidence: “Montague and Capulet, heads of houses at variance with each other” (Dramatis Personae, speech (speech 0)): The conflict is built into the cast list. On characterization: The list sorts Verona into the Prince's family (Escalus, Paris, Mercutio), the Montagues and the Capulets. Mercutio and Paris belong to neither house, which matters when the fighting starts. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
